overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of the design behind current language models. You'll be asked about the context problem, attention, layers and parallel processing, and the context window.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: An older language system reads a long paragraph one word at a time, keeping a running summary of what it has read. Near the end it meets "she" and fails to connect it to a name given in the first line. What best explains the failure?

options.html: The system's vocabulary didn't include the pronoun "she"
options.text: The system's vocabulary didn't include the pronoun "she"
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nothing suggests the word was missing from the vocabulary. In a system that reads in order, an early word reaches a later one only through the running summary, and its trace fades over a long passage.

options.html: The early word's trace faded in the running summary
options.text: The early word's trace faded in the running summary
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A system that reads in order carries context in a summary of fixed size. Details from early in a passage fade as later words arrive, so a long-range dependency can be lost.

options.html: The system chose the wrong meaning at random when it sampled
options.text: The system chose the wrong meaning at random when it sampled
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Sampling concerns how the next token is chosen when writing. The failure here comes from reading in order: the early word's trace faded in the running summary.

options.html: The paragraph was longer than the system's training data
options.text: The paragraph was longer than the system's training data
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The length of the training data isn't the issue. In a system that reads in order, an early word reaches a later one only through the running summary, and its trace fades.

forms.stemHtml: In an attention step, what happens to the representation of a token such as "it"?

options.html: It is replaced by the representation of the nearest noun
options.text: It is replaced by the representation of the nearest noun
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nothing is replaced, and nearness doesn't decide the matter. The token's representation is updated with information from other tokens, weighted by how relevant each one is.

options.html: It is deleted because pronouns carry no meaning
options.text: It is deleted because pronouns carry no meaning
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. No token is deleted. The token's representation is updated with information from other tokens, weighted by how relevant each one is.

options.html: It is checked against a list of grammar rules for pronouns
options.text: It is checked against a list of grammar rules for pronouns
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A transformer stores no grammar rules. The token's representation is updated with information from other tokens, weighted by how relevant each one is.

options.html: It is updated with information from relevant tokens
options.text: It is updated with information from relevant tokens
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Attention lets each token collect information from the others, taking more from those with a high attention weight. Afterward the representation of "it" carries information about what "it" refers to.

forms.stemHtml: Who or what decides which words an attention head links strongly?

options.html: Training, which sets the parameters behind the weights
options.text: Training, which sets the parameters behind the weights
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The numbers that produce attention weights are parameters. They start random, and training adjusts them because useful links lead to better predictions.

options.html: Engineers, who assign each head a relationship to track
options.text: Engineers, who assign each head a relationship to track
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nobody assigns jobs to heads. Training adjusts the parameters behind the weights, and researchers find out afterward what a head has come to track.

options.html: The user, whose prompt tells the model where to look
options.text: The user, whose prompt tells the model where to look
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A prompt supplies the tokens, and it doesn't set how they're weighed. Training adjusts the parameters that produce the weights.

options.html: A dictionary, which lists the words related to each word
options.text: A dictionary, which lists the words related to each word
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. No dictionary is consulted. Training adjusts the parameters that produce the weights.

forms.stemHtml: Why did the transformer make it practical to train much larger models than earlier designs allowed?

options.html: It needs no training data, so there is nothing to wait for
options.text: It needs no training data, so there is nothing to wait for
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Transformers need a great deal of training data. What changed is that all the tokens in a passage are processed at once, so the work of training can be spread across many chips.

options.html: It stores grammar rules, so it has less to learn from text
options.text: It stores grammar rules, so it has less to learn from text
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. No rules are stored. What changed is that all the tokens in a passage are processed at once, so the work of training can be spread across many chips.

options.html: It processes all tokens at once, so chips can share the work
options.text: It processes all tokens at once, so chips can share the work
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Within a layer, every token's update can be computed at the same time. Training can be spread across many chips, so a larger model or more text doesn't mean an impossibly long wait.

options.html: It writes its replies all at once, so it runs faster for users
options.text: It writes its replies all at once, so it runs faster for users
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A model still writes one token at a time. What changed is how a passage is read: all tokens are processed at once, so training can be spread across many chips.

forms.stemHtml: You're in a long conversation with a chatbot that has no memory feature. Which of these are in the model's context window when it writes its next reply? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: The messages you've sent so far in this conversation
options.text: The messages you've sent so far in this conversation
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The conversation so far is sent in again with each new message, as long as it fits.

options.html: A document you pasted in two messages ago
options.text: A document you pasted in two messages ago
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Pasted text is part of the conversation, so it's in the window unless it has been truncated.

options.html: A conversation you had with it last week
options.text: A conversation you had with it last week
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A new conversation starts with nothing from an old one unless a product stores notes and inserts them into the window.

options.html: The model's own earlier replies in this conversation
options.text: The model's own earlier replies in this conversation
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The model's replies are part of the conversation so far, and it predicts from them along with everything else.

options.html: The text the model was trained on
options.text: The text the model was trained on
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Training text shaped the model's parameters. It isn't in the window, and the model doesn't consult it when it writes.

title: The transformer and attention
